steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on semi-supervised crowd counting from unlabeled images. Motivate crowd counting for intelligent transportation, explain why density-based methods need so many labels, review semi-supervised work and its gap, then present our framework and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Crowd counting and intelligent transportation
- Approaches: detection, segmentation, density estimation
- CNN density methods depend on costly labels
- Semi-supervised learning; prior crowd counting work and its gap
- Our approach: self-supervised variation modelling, pseudo labels, GCRU
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - vital in real-world applications; growing impact on intelligent transportation in smart cities (cite)
  - helps human operators get real-time statistics of objects (human traffic) or congestion level
  - transportation planning adjusted; traffic problems solved or avoided
- Approaches
  - focus: image-based crowd scenes (public surveillance), explicit pedestrian counting
  - detection-based (cite), segmentation-based (cite), head density estimation (cite)
  - density-based less sensitive to occlusions in dense crowds -> mainstream
- Label cost
  - CNN main technique for crowd representation + density estimation (cite)
  - promising but rely heavily on labeled data; labour-intensive, time-consuming
  - UCF_QNRF (cite): 2000 human-hours for 1535 images, 1251642 head locations
  - inadequate labels -> overfitting
- Semi-supervised learning
  - reduce overfitting and annotation costs (cite); labelled + unlabelled data
  - used in semantic segmentation (cite), object detection (cite), action recognition (cite)
  - crowd counting: Sindagi et al., Gaussian-Process iterative learning for pseudo labels (cite); Liu et al., surrogate segmentation tasks on unlabeled data (cite)
  - both (cite) show value of unlabelled data but fail to model crowd variations (head scale, illumination, perspective distortion) -> indispensable for reliable modelling
- Our approach
  - model crowd variations self-supervised, two regularization terms
  - pseudo labels for un-annotated data generated, gradually refined
  - joint supervised/unsupervised cost; dynamic weighting across training stages
  - unsupervised pathway: sequence of augmentation functions (image transformations) per unlabeled image
  - Gated-Crowd-Recurrent-Unit (GCRU) for high-order-tensor augmented sequences -> better pseudo labels
  - vs conventional GRU (cite): adds second-order statistics of crowd, informative in crowd modelling (cite)
  - S^{4} Crowd structure in Fig. 1
- Contributions
  - 1. S^{4} Crowd framework: variations modelling, pseudo labeling, dynamic weight training
  - 2. CSE and CEC self-supervised losses
  - 3. GCRU for high-order-tensor crowd sequences, second-order statistics
  - 4. extensive experiments; outperforms other semi-supervised methods

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Crowd counting has a vital role in real-world applications, and in particular its impact on intelligent transportation in smart cities has clearly been increasing. Automatic crowd counting can help human operators directly to get real-time statistics of objects (i.e., human traffic) dynamically and accurately, or the level of congestion, in the various conditions of transportation. With crowd counting, transportation planning can be adjusted effectively and some traffic problems can be solved quickly or avoided.

In this work we focus on estimation for image-based crowd scenes (captured from public surveillance) with explicit counting of pedestrians. The ways of getting the crowd statistics have been explored progressively, from detection-based and segmentation-based approaches to methods based on head density estimation. Density-based methods tended to be less sensitive to occlusions in dense crowds than detection/segmentation-based approaches, and they became the mainstream approaches nowadays.

For density-based methods, Convolution Neural Network (CNN) was the main technique for learning crowd representations and estimating density. Existing CNN-density-based crowd counting methods achieved promising performance, but they relied heavily on labeled data, and getting the labels can be labour-intensive and time-consuming. For example, annotating 1535 images (with 1251642 locations of crowd heads) in the UCF_QNRF dataset took 2000 human-hours. When there are not enough annotated labels, overfitting may happen.

To reduce the overfitting and the annotation costs, semi-supervised learning, which can use both labelled and unlabelled data, has been widely used in many computer vision tasks like semantic segmentation, object detection and action recognition. Most recently semi-supervised learning was also used in the crowd counting community. Sindagi et al. proposed a Gaussian-Process iterative learning to estimate pseudo labels for unlabeled crowd data, and Liu et al. proposed learning the crowd representation from unlabeled data with some surrogate segmentation tasks. Both works showed that it is effective to leverage the unlabelled crowd data, but their semi-supervised schemes failed to model the variations of crowds (e.g., head scale, illumination, perspective distortion, etc.), and these are considered indispensable factors for reliable crowd modelling.

- Our approach
  - model crowd variations self-supervised, two regularization terms
  - pseudo labels of un-annotated data generated and gradually refined
  - joint supervised/unsupervised cost function; dynamic weighting at different training stages
  - unsupervised pathway: sequence of augmentation functions (image transformations) on each unlabeled image
  - GCRU (Gated-Crowd-Recurrent-Unit) to encode high-order-tensor augmented sequences -> high-quality pseudo labels
  - vs conventional GRU: second-order statistics of crowd, informative for crowd modelling
  - S^{4} Crowd structure in Fig. 1
- Contributions
  - 1. S^{4} Crowd framework (variations modelling, pseudo labeling, dynamic weight training) for limited labels
  - 2. CSE + CEC self-supervised losses for crowd variations
  - 3. GCRU: high-order-tensor crowd sequences, second-order statistics
  - 4. extensive experiments, components studied; beats other semi-supervised crowd counting methods

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Crowd counting has a vital role in real-world applications, and in particular its impact on intelligent transportation in smart cities has clearly been increasing. Automatic crowd counting can help human operators directly to get real-time statistics of objects (i.e., human traffic) dynamically and accurately, or the level of congestion, in the various conditions of transportation. With crowd counting, transportation planning can be adjusted effectively and some traffic problems can be solved quickly or avoided.

In this work we focus on estimation for image-based crowd scenes (captured from public surveillance) with explicit counting of pedestrians. The ways of getting the crowd statistics have been explored progressively, from detection-based and segmentation-based approaches to methods based on head density estimation. Density-based methods tended to be less sensitive to occlusions in dense crowds than detection/segmentation-based approaches, and they became the mainstream approaches nowadays.

For density-based methods, Convolution Neural Network (CNN) was the main technique for learning crowd representations and estimating density. Existing CNN-density-based crowd counting methods achieved promising performance, but they relied heavily on labeled data, and getting the labels can be labour-intensive and time-consuming. For example, annotating 1535 images (with 1251642 locations of crowd heads) in the UCF_QNRF dataset took 2000 human-hours. When there are not enough annotated labels, overfitting may happen.

To reduce the overfitting and the annotation costs, semi-supervised learning, which can use both labelled and unlabelled data, has been widely used in many computer vision tasks like semantic segmentation, object detection and action recognition. Most recently semi-supervised learning was also used in the crowd counting community. Sindagi et al. proposed a Gaussian-Process iterative learning to estimate pseudo labels for unlabeled crowd data, and Liu et al. proposed learning the crowd representation from unlabeled data with some surrogate segmentation tasks. Both works showed that it is effective to leverage the unlabelled crowd data, but their semi-supervised schemes failed to model the variations of crowds (e.g., head scale, illumination, perspective distortion, etc.), and these are considered indispensable factors for reliable crowd modelling.

To address this issue we proposed to model the different crowd variations in a self-supervised way, with two regularization terms. At the same time the pseudo labels of the un-annotated data were generated and refined gradually for better model generalization. In our semi-supervised scheme we proposed a joint cost function that includes both the supervised and the unsupervised loss, and we used a dynamic weighting strategy to balance the two losses at different training stages.

In the unsupervised pathway, a sequence of augmentation functions (i.e., image transformations) was applied to each unlabeled image to simulate different variations. We proposed a new recurrent unit, called Gated-Crowd-Recurrent-Unit (GCRU), to better encode the high-order-tensor augmented image sequences so that high-quality pseudo labels can be generated. GCRU also considered the second-order statistics of the crowd compared with the conventional GRU, and these were shown to be informative features in crowd modelling. The general structure of our proposed S^{4} Crowd is shown in Fig. 1. Our main contributions in this work are:

- 1. We proposed a new semi-supervised crowd counting framework, S^{4} Crowd, which included several key components (variations modelling, pseudo labeling, a dynamic weight training scheme) for robust crowd modelling with limited labeled data.

- 2. We proposed two self-supervised losses/regularisation terms, Crowd Scale Equivariance (CSE) and Crowd Entropy Consistency (CEC), and we used them to model the crowd variations in an unsupervised way.

- 3. We proposed a crowd-driven recurrent unit, Gated-Crowd-Recurrent-Unit (GCRU), to encode high-order-tensor crowd sequences, which can also learn the informative second-order crowd statistics for better crowd modelling.

- 4. We conducted extensive experiments and studied the proposed components of our semi-supervised S^{4} Crowd framework. Our method outperformed other semi-supervised crowd counting algorithms in various settings.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Crowd counting plays a vital role in real-world applications; specifically, it has had an obviously increasing impact on intelligent transportation in smart cities [1,2,3,4]. Automatic crowd counting can directly help human operators to dynamically and accurately obtain real-time statistics of objects (i.e., human traffic) or the level of congestion in the various conditions of transportation. With the help of crowd counting, transportation planning can be effectively adjusted and some traffic problems can be quickly solved or avoided.

In this work, we focus on image-based crowd scene (captured from public surveillance) estimation with explicit pedestrian counting. The ways of obtaining crowd statistics have been progressively explored, from detection-based [5] and segmentation-based approaches [6] to head density estimation based methods [7]. Compared with detection/segmentation-based approaches, density-based methods tended to be less sensitive to occlusions in dense crowds, and they became the mainstream approaches nowadays.

For density-based methods, Convolution Neural Network (CNN) was the major technique [8,9] for crowd representation learning and density estimation. While existing CNN-density-based crowd counting methods achieved promising performance, they relied heavily on labeled data, and the acquisition of labels can be labour-intensive and time-consuming. For example, it took 2000 human-hours to annotate 1535 images (with 1251642 locations of crowd heads) in the UCF_QNRF dataset [10]. With inadequate annotated labels, overfitting may occur.

To reduce the overfitting effect and the annotation costs [1,2,3,4], semi-supervised learning, which can take advantage of both labelled and unlabelled data, has been widely used in many computer vision tasks such as semantic segmentation [11], object detection [12] and action recognition [13]. Most recently, semi-supervised learning was also employed in the crowd counting community. Sindagi et al. proposed a Gaussian-Process iterative learning to estimate the pseudo labels for unlabeled crowd data [14], and Liu et al. proposed to learn the crowd representation from unlabeled data with some surrogate segmentation tasks [15]. Both works [14,15] demonstrated the effectiveness of leveraging the unlabelled crowd data, yet their semi-supervised schemes failed to model the variations of crowds (e.g., head scale, illumination, perspective distortion, etc.), which are considered indispensable factors for reliable crowd modelling.

To address this issue, we proposed to model different crowd variations in a self-supervised manner, specifically with two regularization terms. In the meantime, the pseudo labels of the un-annotated data were generated and gradually refined for better model generalization. In our semi-supervised scheme, a joint cost function including both supervised and unsupervised losses was proposed, and a dynamic weighting strategy was employed to balance both losses at different training stages.

Specifically, in the unsupervised pathway, a sequence of augmentation functions (i.e., image transformations) was applied to each unlabeled image to simulate different variations. To better encode the high-order-tensor augmented image sequences for high-quality pseudo label generation, we proposed a novel recurrent unit, namely the Gated-Crowd-Recurrent-Unit (GCRU). Compared with the conventional GRU [16], GCRU further considered the second-order statistics of the crowd, which have been demonstrated to be informative features in crowd modelling [17]. The general structure of our proposed S^{4} Crowd is shown in Fig. 1. In this work, our main contributions can be summarised as:

- 1. We proposed a novel semi-supervised crowd counting framework, S^{4} Crowd, which included several key components (variations modelling, pseudo labeling, dynamic weight training scheme) for robust crowd modelling with limited labeled data.

- 2. We proposed two self-supervised losses/regularisation terms, i.e., Crowd Scale Equivariance (CSE) and Crowd Entropy Consistency (CEC), based on which we modelled the crowd variations in an unsupervised manner.

- 3. A crowd-driven recurrent unit, i.e., the Gated-Crowd-Recurrent-Unit (GCRU), was proposed to encode high-order-tensor crowd sequences; it can also learn the informative second-order crowd statistics for better crowd modelling.

- 4. Extensive experiments were conducted, and the proposed components of our semi-supervised S^{4} Crowd framework were well studied. Our method outperformed other semi-supervised crowd counting algorithms in various settings.
